Training language models whose parameters and optimizer state exceed a single node’s memory requires sharding these tensors across devices. Under tensor parallelism (TP) or fully sharded data parallelism (FSDP), matrix-aware optimizers such as Muon introduce communication to perform global matrix operations across shards. We propose Dobb ( D istributed O ptimizer with B lock-diagonal Eigen b ases), a matrix-aware optimizer designed to compute updates locally within parameter shards. Dobb approximates the input-activation second moment with diagonal blocks and tracks a complete basis within each block. It projects momentum into these bases, applies sign normalization to the coefficients, and reconstructs the update. When each block lies within one shard under TP or FSDP, Dobb applies its matrix update locally, requiring no communication beyond data-parallel synchronization of the activation second moments. We benchmark Dobb against Dion, a distributed matrix-aware optimizer designed to retain the benefits of orthonormalized updates while reducing communication. On GPT-2 XL (1.56B parameters), Dobb with 16 blocks reaches a validation loss of 2.476, compared with 2.511 for Dion at rank fraction 1/16. Under FSDP on 32 H100 GPUs, Dobb reduces the amortized optimizer-call time from 124.1 ms for Dion to 9.2 ms.

Language-model scaling increases the memory requirements for parameters, gradients, and optimizer state ( Kaplan et al., 2020 ; Rajbhandari et al., 2020 ) . When these quantities exceed a single GPU’s capacity, training distributes them across devices through tensor parallelism (TP) or fully sharded data parallelism (FSDP) ( Shoeybi et al., 2019 ; Zhao et al., 2023 ) . Under either layout, each device holds one part of every sharded weight matrix, and we call this part a shard; data-parallel replicas hold copies of the same shards. Cross-shard communication is communication among the devices that hold different shards of one matrix. These layouts make matrix-aware optimization a distributed problem: an update defined on a complete weight matrix may require information held by several devices. Muon orthogonalizes momentum ( Jordan et al., 2024 ) , which introduces dense optimizer-specific communication in conventional sharded implementations ( Ahn et al., 2025 ; Khaled et al., 2026 ) . MuonBP reduces communication by performing local Newton–Schulz orthogonalization between periodic global steps, but those global steps still require full cross-shard communication ( Khaled et al., 2026 ) . The frequency of global orthogonalization controls the tradeoff between communication cost and optimization quality. Another approach, Dion, reduces the size of each exchange by approximating momentum with low-rank factors and retaining the residual through error feedback ( Ahn et al., 2025 ) . Its optimizer step communicates these factors across shards, so communication scales with the update rank.

In this work, we introduce Dobb ( D istributed O ptimizer with B lock-diagonal Eigen b ases) to reduce optimizer communication. We approximate the activation second moment by a block-diagonal matrix and retain a complete eigenbasis within every block. This construction discards cross-block correlations without imposing a reduced-rank constraint on the update. When these blocks align with shard boundaries, the optimizer step requires no cross-shard communication beyond the data-parallel synchronization of the activation second moments. Dion derives its low-rank factors from momentum; we instead project momentum onto an input-side basis from an exponentially averaged activation second moment, normalize the coefficients, and reconstruct the update. For a mini-batch gradient, projection into its own activation eigenbasis separates input spectral scales from the output-gradient structure, leaving the latter in the coefficients (Section 3 ). In our GPT-2 Small experiments, activation second moments exhibit greater spectral concentration than output-gradient second moments in most matched matrices (Figure 2 ). This motivates using the activation eigenbasis to expose the more concentrated factor’s directional scaling for normalization (Appendix F.2 ).

Both sign and column normalization remove positive input spectral scales from a mini-batch gradient expressed in its own activation eigenbasis. We choose the element-wise sign, which additionally removes magnitude differences within each coefficient column. In our synthetic comparison, this choice produces more orthogonal updates than column normalization except when the output-gradient spectrum is nearly flat (Table 1 ). Sign normalization also avoids the norm reduction required by column normalization when the output axis is sharded, because it acts on each coefficient independently. We make four contributions: • We introduce Dobb, which normalizes momentum coefficients in block-diagonal activation second-moment eigenbases while retaining every direction within each block. • Dobb requires only that each block lie within one shard. Under this condition, the optimizer step introduces zero optimizer-specific cross-shard bytes beyond the data-parallel synchronization of the activation second moments. • We compare Dobb with Muon and Dion on GPT-2-style models up to 1.56B parameters under a shared update-scale protocol. Across these scales, Dobb exhibits less validation-loss degradation under block partitioning than Dion under corresponding rank reductions. • We benchmark Dobb against Muon and Dion under FSDP and tensor parallelism on GPT-2-style models up to 8.1B parameters and on Qwen3 models up to 32B. In every measured configuration, Dobb’s optimizer call is shorter than those of Muon and Dion (Section 6.2 ).

Matrix-aware optimizers use the intrinsic two-dimensional structure of weight matrices to construct parameter updates rather than treating each entry independently. Muon orthogonalizes momentum using Newton–Schulz iterations, while RMNP uses row normalization ( Jordan et al., 2024 ; Deng et al., 2026 ) . K-FAC builds a Kronecker-factored approximation to layerwise curvature ( Martens and Grosse, 2015 ) . Shampoo accumulates gradient-derived matrix second moments, and SOAP applies Adam in their eigenbases ( Gupta et al., 2018 ; Vyas et al., 2025 ) .

ZeRO reduces memory redundancy across data-parallel workers by progressively sharding optimizer state, gradients, and parameters across its three stages ( Rajbhandari et al., 2020 ) . FSDP shards all three and gathers parameters as needed for forward and backward computation ( Zhao et al., 2023 ) . FSDP2 uses per-parameter sharding, which facilitates composition with tensor parallelism ( Liang et al., 2025 ) . Tensor parallelism, as used in Megatron-LM, partitions weight matrices and their matrix multiplications across devices ( Shoeybi et al., 2019 ) . The resulting parameter layout determines which operands are local and which require communication during the optimizer step.

While element-wise optimizer updates parallelize naturally, matrix-aware updates introduce dependencies among optimizer state, matrix computations, and the underlying parameter layout. Dion retains a full-size momentum buffer distributed across shards and reduces communication through low-rank factor operations and error feedback, with communication scaling with the update rank ( Ahn et al., 2025 ) . Distributed Shampoo takes a different approach. It distributes preconditioner state and computation by parameter block within data-parallel process groups, then all-gathers the computed search directions within each group at every optimizer step ( Shi et al., 2023 ) . MatrixFSDP takes a systems approach under FSDP: it places each whole matrix on one owner rank, so Muon runs unchanged without optimizer-step collectives, and it leaves matrices sharded by tensor parallelism outside its scope ( Gao et al., 2026 ) .

We seek a basis for normalizing momentum coefficients while keeping the optimizer step local to parameter shards. We motivate the basis source, normalization, and block partition through gradient structure, spectral comparisons, and the distributed parameter layout.

chunks.section: Spectral concentration motivates the input-side basis.
chunks.text: In transformer training, weight gradients ( Shen et al., 2026 ) and updates from SGD with momentum and Adam ( Jordan et al., 2024 ) typically have low-rank structure. Muon approximately orthogonalizes its updates, making their singular values nearly equal, and achieves model quality comparable to AdamW with less compute ( Jordan et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025 ) . We compare activation and output-gradient second moments using entropy-based effective rank, normalized by the factor dimension, across layer types and training checkpoints (Figure 2 ). A lower effective rank indicates that the spectrum is concentrated in fewer eigendirections. Figure 2 shows that activation factors exhibit greater spectral concentration than the corresponding output-gradient factors. Shen et al. (2026) report highly concentrated singular values in the input feature matrices of MNIST and CIFAR-10 and in RoBERTa text embeddings. K-FAC exploits slowly changing second-moment factors and relatively stable curvature to amortize inverse computations across optimizer steps ( Martens and Grosse, 2015 , Appendix G) . Following this rationale, we reuse the activation-side basis between periodic refreshes, reducing the amortized cost of basis computation. Appendix F.4 evaluates the resulting tradeoff between iteration time and optimization quality.

Under TP and FSDP alike, each rank holds one shard of a weight matrix and the matching shards of its gradient and optimizer state, so a matrix-aware update of the complete matrix needs operands from other shards. We therefore seek a basis that each rank can construct and apply from its own operands: a block-diagonal basis whose blocks align with shard boundaries. We write TP \mathrm{TP} for the tensor-parallel degree, FS \mathrm{FS} for the FSDP shard degree, and B B for the number of second-moment blocks. In the Megatron-LM layout, a column-parallel layer shards the output axis m m and receives a replicated input, whereas a row-parallel layer shards the input axis n n and reduces partial outputs ( Shoeybi et al., 2019 ) . For row-parallel layers, we partition the activation second moment into diagonal blocks within the input shards, so each block basis acts on local momentum columns. For column-parallel layers, the replicated input allows each rank to construct the same block bases and apply them to its local momentum rows. Under FSDP, our implementation shards each matrix that Dobb updates along its input axis, so each rank holds whole blocks and their momentum columns, as in a row-parallel layer. This construction accommodates both sharding axes under TP and the input-axis sharding under FSDP without requiring cross-shard communication during the optimizer step beyond the data-parallel synchronization of the activation second moments. This synchronization spans FSDP ranks and data-parallel replicas, which process different data, but not the ranks of a TP group, which share their data (Section 5 ).

chunks.section: Block partitioning retains a complete basis.
chunks.text: The activation spectrum motivates the choice of basis, while sharding under TP and FSDP constrains how we construct and apply it. Dion reduces communication through low-rank updates, restricting each update to a lower-dimensional subspace while retaining the approximation residual through error feedback ( Ahn et al., 2025 ) . A rank- r r update has at least min ⁡ ( m , n ) − r \min(m,n)-r zero singular values, which limits its orthogonality over the full matrix space even when its factors have orthonormal columns. We instead partition the activation second moment into B B blocks and retain all eigenvectors within each block. This construction discards cross-block correlations without imposing a reduced-rank constraint on the update and allows basis operations to remain local when blocks align with shard boundaries. At B = n B=n , each block holds one input coordinate, each block basis is ± 1 \pm 1 , and the update reduces to sign ⁡ ( 𝑴 ) / m \operatorname{sign}({\bm{M}})/\sqrt{m} , sign descent with momentum ( Bernstein et al., 2018 ) . As B B increases from 1 to n n , Dobb’s update therefore moves from normalization in a single activation eigenbasis toward sign descent with momentum, whereas reducing Dion’s rank increases the number of zero singular values in its update.

Dobb normalizes momentum in a second-moment eigenbasis whose blocks can be assigned to individual shards. All eigenvectors within each block are retained; B B controls the block partition. Algorithm 1 states Dobb for one weight matrix.

When each block lies within one shard, projection, element-wise sign normalization, and reconstruction use local operands. Section 5 derives the resulting cross-shard payload and accounts separately for data-parallel second-moment synchronization.

We count optimizer-specific cross-shard communication separately from the synchronization of second moments across data-parallel ranks. All communication counts in this section, including Table 3 , describe logical payloads. We assume the Megatron-LM layout of Section 3 under TP and, under either layout, that each block of Dobb lies within one shard. When neither axis of a matrix is sharded, as under data parallelism alone, cross-shard communication is zero for every optimizer.

For Dobb on a row-parallel layer, or under FSDP with the input-axis sharding of Section 3 , each input block and its momentum columns reside on the same rank. On a column-parallel layer the input is replicated, so each rank can form every input-side block basis and apply it to its own momentum rows. chunks.section: FSDP has a separate synchronization requirement.
chunks.text: FSDP ranks process different data, so consistent second moments require aggregation across the data-parallel group even when each block lies within one shard. The ranks of a TP group process the same data, so this aggregation does not cross TP ranks. Dobb captures and synchronizes its block second moments only on refresh iterations, once every T T optimizer steps; the other optimizer steps issue no optimizer collective. Our implementation reduce-scatters the block second moments across the FSDP ranks, followed by an all-reduce across data-parallel replicas when the FSDP group is replicated. Each rank then refreshes the bases of its own blocks, so no bases are exchanged. Each refresh synchronizes n 2 / B n^{2}/B second-moment entries per matrix (Appendix C ), separately from the cross-shard count above.

For Dobb, projection and reconstruction cost 𝒪 ⁡ ( m ​ n 2 / B ) \mathcal{O}(mn^{2}/B) , while one orthogonal iteration per refresh costs 𝒪 ⁡ ( n 3 / ( B 2 ​ T ) ) \mathcal{O}(n^{3}/(B^{2}T)) amortized. Capturing N c N_{c} token positions once per refresh adds 𝒪 ⁡ ( N c ​ n 2 / ( B ​ T ) ) \mathcal{O}(N_{c}n^{2}/(BT)) . Storing the second moment and full block basis requires 2 ​ n 2 / B 2n^{2}/B scalars, in addition to momentum. Small products, basis orthogonalization, and communication overlap determine the realized cost.

Including momentum and the block second moment, Dobb stores n 2 + 2 ​ n 2 / B n^{2}+2n^{2}/B scalars, while Dion stores n 2 + n 2 / B n^{2}+n^{2}/B . chunks.section: 6.2 Iteration time under FSDP and tensor parallelism
chunks.text: We measured iteration time on GPT-2-style models from 772M to 8.1B parameters with our FSDP and TP implementation, and on Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-32B ( Yang and others, 2025 ) with an implementation built on the open-source Dion codebase ( Ahn et al., 2025 ) . Both implementations use PyTorch FSDP2 with DTensor-based TP ( Liang et al., 2025 ) . In all timing runs, NCCL communicated between nodes over TCP sockets. Table 5 reports one configuration per model and GPU type; Appendix G gives the setups and the remaining configurations. Because Dobb’s forward-backward overhead lies within the run-to-run variation of forward-backward time, the table reports pooled iteration times, which share one forward-backward estimate per configuration and add each method’s measured optimizer call (Appendix G.1 ). In Table 5 , Dobb’s amortized optimizer call takes 6.9 to 16.3 ms on GPT-2 and 86.2 to 168.0 ms on Qwen3, against 82.7 to 2782.1 ms for Muon and 159.5 to 2523.2 ms for Dion. Muon’s pooled iteration time is 1.07 to 1.52 times that of Dobb, and Dion’s is 1.07 to 1.59 times. The quality runs and the timing runs both include GPT-2 XL with B = 16 B=16 for Dobb and Dion at the corresponding rank fraction 1 / 16 1/16 . In this configuration, Dobb reaches a validation loss of 2.476 against 2.511 for Dion (Table 4 ), and under FSDP on 32 H100 GPUs, its amortized optimizer call takes 9.2 ms against 124.1 ms, with pooled iteration times of 1069.1 and 1184.0 ms (Table 23 ).

We introduce Dobb, which normalizes momentum coefficients in block-diagonal activation second-moment eigenbases. The central design choice is to discard cross-block correlations while retaining every basis direction within each block. Together with element-wise sign normalization, this construction introduces zero optimizer-specific cross-shard bytes when each block lies within one shard, beyond the data-parallel synchronization of the block second moments. Across GPT-2 Small, Medium, Large, and XL, Dobb exhibits less validation-loss degradation under block partitioning than Dion under corresponding rank reductions. Dobb’s optimizer call is shorter than those of Muon and Dion in every measured FSDP and TP configuration (Appendix G ). These timing runs are short and report pooled iteration times. Further work could investigate how block size and basis-refresh frequency should vary across layers and training stages. Because Dobb’s basis refresh reads no gradient, it could also move out of the optimizer call into idle intervals of forward-backward computation and communication (Appendix G.2 ). Understanding how discarded cross-block correlations and coefficient normalization theoretically affect optimization could also guide block partitions that preserve useful structure while respecting shard boundaries.

chunks.text: Second-moment capture uses forward hooks for side A A and backward hooks for side G G . The hooks are inactive outside training mode and on non-refresh iterations, and they accumulate the block outer products in place, so captured activations or output gradients are not retained after the hook returns. Column normalization in the ℓ 2 \ell_{2} variants sums squares over a full coefficient column; when that axis is sharded, the sum requires one reduction across the shards, which Section 5 counts separately from the local update. The principal settings are β C = 0.95 \beta_{C}=0.95 , μ = 0.95 \mu=0.95 , T = 9 T=9 , one warm orthogonal iteration, fp32 second-moment accumulation, and bf16 basis storage. Appendix F.8 compares these two precision choices against their alternatives. Appendix F.5 compares the single orthogonal iteration with two and three iterations and with an exact eigendecomposition. The shift for the cold-start eigendecomposition and Householder QR is ε = 10 − 6 \varepsilon=10^{-6} in the stated accumulation convention. The scale constant is τ = 0.2 \tau=0.2 , and weight decay is λ = 0.1 \lambda=0.1 . Table 8 lists the selected learning rates.

Algorithm 3 specifies three alternative configurations that change the basis source or coefficient normalization of Dobb, and Appendix F compares them. With each block within one shard, sign normalization requires no cross-shard reduction for either basis source. Column normalization changes this result only when its reduction axis is sharded. Dobb- ℓ 2 \ell_{2} reduces one squared norm for each of n n coefficient columns when the output axis is sharded. Dobb-G- ℓ 2 \ell_{2} reduces m m such values when the input axis is sharded. Independent norm reductions can be packed to reduce collective-launch overhead. For a square 4096 × 4096 4096\times 4096 matrix in fp32, these 4096 scalars contain 0.0164 MB. chunks.section: Appendix G Details of the distributed iteration-time experiments
chunks.text: This appendix gives the settings and the full timing breakdown of the four campaigns summarized in Table 5 . Three campaigns used our implementation, built on PyTorch FSDP2 with DTensor-based TP [ Liang et al., 2025 ] : GPT-2 Large and XL on A5000 GPUs (Appendix G.3 ), GPT-2 XL on H100 GPUs, and GPT-2 3B, 6B, and 8B on H100 GPUs (Appendix G.4 ). The fourth campaign timed Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-32B on H100 GPUs with an implementation built on the open-source Dion codebase [ Ahn et al., 2025 ] , which we call the Dion-based implementation (Appendix G.5 ). It also uses PyTorch FSDP2 with DTensor-based TP. For Qwen3, this appendix also reports timings for the output-gradient basis with column normalization, Dobb-G- ℓ 2 \ell_{2} , defined in Algorithm 3 . All four campaigns used NCCL over TCP sockets between nodes. The optimizer-call times are measured, and the pooled iteration times are derived from measured means; the communication counts in Section 5 are analytical, and the tables report times only. Pooled iteration time is the comparison metric (Appendix G.1 ). In every campaign, Dobb refreshes its bases every T = 9 T=9 iterations. Both Qwen3 series use the fixed-count partition of Appendix B , with B = FS B=\mathrm{FS} blocks per weight matrix. Each Qwen3 series pairs Dion’s rank fraction with a width of 1024 / FS 1024/\mathrm{FS} , following the width–rank match of Section 5 . In the GPT-2 campaigns, Dobb’s blocks follow the shards, so each block lies within one shard.

chunks.section: Appendix G Details of the distributed iteration-time experiments
chunks.text: Our implementation applies the matrix optimizers to the two-dimensional weights of the transformer blocks and AdamW to the remaining parameters. It runs a distributed Muon [ Jordan et al., 2024 ] that orthogonalizes each whole weight matrix with Newton–Schulz iterations. Every GPT-2 run started from a random initialization, used a global batch of 480 OpenWebText sequences of 1024 tokens, and kept the gathered FSDP weights across accumulation micro-steps. Our implementation compiles the model with torch.compile , whereas the Dion-based implementation disables model compilation; both log timings on one rank.

At a given model and device mesh, the forward-backward pass performs the same model computation for every optimizer; for Dobb it also contains the second-moment capture on refresh iterations and the reduction of the captured second moments, which our implementation launches from the capture hook behind the backward pass. We measured the run-to-run variation of forward-backward time on GPT-2 Large at FS = 10 \mathrm{FS}=10 , TP = 2 \mathrm{TP}=2 on 20 A5000 GPUs in three allocations, each running AdamW, Muon, Dion r = 400 r=400 , and Dobb once in each of four rounds, for 48 runs of 30 timed iterations; the run order was fixed in one allocation and balanced over position and predecessor by a Williams Latin square in the other two. Table 20 compares the forward-backward pass means and their run-to-run variation. Dobb’s mean forward-backward time of 7740 ms lies between the lowest and highest baseline means, 7713 ms for Dion and 7788 ms for Muon. After round and method effects within each allocation are removed, a run’s mean forward-backward time has a standard deviation of 16.6 ms (0.21%). In the 12 pairs of Dobb and AdamW runs from the same round, Dobb’s forward-backward mean exceeds AdamW’s by 16.8 ms (0.22%) on average, with a 95% confidence interval of 2.4 to 31.3 ms; this overhead is comparable to the run-to-run standard deviation and small against the variation of a single pair’s difference, about ± 51 \pm 51 ms at the 95% level. Dobb’s mean iteration time exceeds AdamW’s by 13.6 ms (0.18%), with a 95% confidence interval of − 1.1 -1.1 to 28.4 ms that includes zero. Muon’s and Dion’s mean iteration times exceed AdamW’s by 672 ms (8.68%) and 1209 ms (15.61%). Thus, Dobb’s total iteration-time overhead is indistinguishable from network timing noise in these runs. To compare optimizer-step costs more fairly in the presence of this noise, we compute pooled iteration times by adding each method’s measured optimizer-call mean to shared estimates of forward-backward time and the remaining iteration time, each averaged over all reported runs of the same configuration. Each method then adds its own measured optimizer-call mean, so within a configuration, pooled iteration times differ only by the optimizer call, and pooling excludes optimizer-specific work inside forward-backward, including Dobb’s capture and reduction. In the Qwen3-32B runs, the Dion-based TP implementation reduces Dobb’s second moments inside the optimizer call instead (Appendix G.5 ), so there pooling excludes only the capture. For Dobb, the optimizer-call mean is averaged over one refresh cycle, ( Refresh + 8 ⋅ Non-refresh ) / 9 (\text{Refresh}+8\cdot\text{Non-refresh})/9 .

chunks.section: G.2 Work that can leave the optimizer call
chunks.text: An operation can leave the optimizer call once its inputs are available if it does not require the current mini-batch weight gradient. Table 21 classifies the operations of the compared optimizers and of Shampoo, SOAP, and K-FAC by this criterion. Every operation of AdamW, Muon, and the standard Dion update reads the gradient. The lazy variant of Dion refreshes its right factor only every k k steps, and the CPU variant computes this refresh on CPUs from the momentum of earlier steps while forward-backward runs on the GPUs [ Ahn et al., 2025 , Section 5.1] . Shampoo and SOAP accumulate their statistics from the gradient, so their inverse roots or eigenbases can leave the optimizer call only if they use statistics from earlier steps. SOAP recomputes its eigenbases at the end of a step and first uses them in the next [ Vyas et al., 2025 , Algorithm 3] , and Shi et al. [2023] describe a JAX implementation of Shampoo that overlaps the root-inverse computation, offloaded to CPUs, with updates that use stale roots. K-FAC and Dobb estimate their statistics from activations and output gradients instead, so neither their statistics nor the inverses or bases derived from them read the gradient of any step. Martens and Grosse [2015] obtain the K-FAC output-gradient factor from an additional backward pass with sampled targets (their Section 5), recompute the inverses every 20 iterations in their experiments, and note that these computations can run simultaneously with the gradient computation (their Section 8).

chunks.section: Scheduling Dobb’s work outside the optimizer call.
chunks.text: The refresh reads only the block second moments and the previous basis (Algorithm 2 ), yet both implementations run it inside the optimizer call on refresh iterations. For the activation-side basis, the refresh of a weight matrix could start once its second moment has been captured and reduced, while forward-backward computation continues for other layers. Work moved out of the optimizer call still occupies the GPUs, so it shortens the iteration only to the extent that it fills intervals in which they would otherwise wait; we did not measure this overlap. Osawa et al. [2023] assign the curvature and inversion work of K-FAC to the bubbles of pipeline-parallel schedules and refresh the curvature once every few steps, so that preconditioning is the only added computation. Explicit scheduling of Dobb’s capture, reduction, and basis refresh into idle intervals remains future work.
